title: Kapila Teaches His Mother
hookLine: Devahuti asks her son Kapila to end her sorrow, and Samkhya begins with three kinds of pain
carry: three kinds of pain, and knowing ends them

cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, a woman named Devahuti has spent long years serving a sage, Kardama. When their son is born, the sage, his promise kept, leaves for the forest. Devahuti is left at home with the boy, Kapila.

And she knows something about him: the Bhagavata says he is Vishnu himself, come to teach. So one day she sits before her own son and asks for help. I'm tired, she says, of senses that never stop wanting.
They've pulled me into the dark. You're the light I need. Cut through this confusion.
A mother asking her child for wisdom. Kapila smiles, and begins.

teach.b: Tradition names Kapila as the source of Samkhya, the school that opens today.

The Bhagavata's Kapila teaches it with love of God at the center; the school's oldest surviving book, Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika, sets it out on its own. Both start where Devahuti started: with pain.

The Karika's first verse says: because we're struck by three kinds of pain, we want to know what ends it. Commentators sort them: pain from within, in body and mind; pain from other beings; and pain from forces beyond us.
Then an objector asks: why philosophy? There's medicine. The Karika doesn't call medicine bad.
It says the seen remedies aren't certain and aren't final; the pain comes back. Even rituals, it says, help but wear off.

teach.h: KNOW THE WORLD, AND THE KNOWER.
teach.b: What ends pain is knowing: what's manifest, what's unmanifest, and the knower. In the Bhagavata, Kapila tells his mother the same thing in his own way: the mind is what binds and what frees.
Caught in the world's three strands, it binds; turned toward the Lord, it frees. And you've heard this teaching before.
When Hindus close a prayer with Om shanti, shanti, shanti, many teachers explain the three as peace from those same three kinds of pain: from within, from others, from the world.
So the doctor and the medicine are real, and Samkhya keeps them. It just says the deepest peace comes from seeing clearly who is suffering.

how: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and taught alongside Yoga, its paired school. Kapila's teaching to Devahuti fills chapters of the Bhagavata's third book, and many Hindus close prayers with Om shanti, shanti, shanti, often explained as peace from the three kinds of pain.

games.q: you're the objector in the Samkhya Karika. you say: "why study philosophy? there are remedies for pain." what does the text answer?
o: remedies are wrong, and you should give them up.
remedies help, but they aren't certain or final.
pain isn't real, so there's nothing to remedy.
games.why: the Karika doesn't throw out medicine. it says the seen remedies aren't certain or final, and that knowing is better.

practice: Bring to mind one pain you're carrying and simply sort it: from within, from another person, or from the world. Then, if you pray, say Om shanti, shanti, shanti softly, one shanti for each kind, the way many Hindus close a prayer.
If you don't pray, name each kind and let one long breath out after it. If a pain is ever too heavy, or you think of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Samkhya. The school tradition traces to Kapila. It begins with three kinds of pain, and says knowing, not only fixing, is what ends them.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Samkhya, the school whose name some take as counting, others as discernment.

carryVoice: Your line: three kinds of pain, and knowing ends them. Kapila's first student was his mother. Same time tomorrow.
